lines.say: Here is a puzzle. Two different qubits look alike whenever we measure them.
Both read zero half the time and one half the time. How can we tell them apart?
Think of polarized sunglasses. They only let through light that wiggles their way.
Send in light wiggling on a slant, and upright glasses pass only half.
Tilt the glasses to that slant, and all of it passes.
The light never changed. Only the question the glasses were asking did.
A qubit works the same way. Picture it as an arrow inside a ball.
Measuring asks about one line through the ball, called an axis, usually with zero at the top and one at the bottom.
Our two qubits point sideways, to the front and the back. We call them plus and minus.
Both sit halfway between top and bottom, so asking up or down gives fifty fifty.
Ask along the front to back axis instead, and plus answers plus every time, while minus answers minus.
But real hardware can only ask up or down.
So first we turn it with an H gate, which swaps front and back with up and down.
Now plus reads zero and minus reads one, every time.
Here the sunglasses picture breaks. A beam can partly pass, but one particle of light passes or it doesn't.
Fifty fifty doesn't mean the qubit is random. Plus is perfectly definite, just not lined up with the question.
A measurement asks about one axis. To ask about another, turn that axis onto up and down first.
